blocks.body: The **Pauli-X gate** is the quantum equivalent of a classical NOT gate. It flips a qubit's state: |0⟩ becomes |1⟩, and |1⟩ becomes |0⟩. It's the simplest single-qubit gate and the first one every quantum programmer learns.
The X gate is named after physicist Wolfgang Pauli. Together with the Y and Z gates, the three Pauli gates form a basis for all single-qubit operations.
Every quantum gate is represented by a unitary matrix. The X gate's matrix is:
This matrix swaps the amplitudes of |0⟩ and |1⟩. When we apply it to a general qubit state:
Let's see what happens when we apply the X gate to |0⟩:

blocks.caption: X gate flips |0⟩ to |1⟩ — the probability of measuring |1⟩ is 100%

blocks.body: And when we apply X twice (X on |1⟩):
Applying X twice returns the qubit to its original state. This makes sense — flipping a bit twice gives you back the original!

blocks.caption: Two X gates cancel out — the qubit returns to |0⟩

blocks.body: The X gate performs a **π rotation around the X-axis** of the Bloch sphere. This takes |0⟩ (north pole) to |1⟩ (south pole) and vice versa.

blocks.body: **Key takeaway:** The X gate is the quantum NOT. It flips |0⟩ ↔ |1⟩. Applying it twice returns the qubit to its original state (X² = I).
